## Today's session

Today we will use simple plots to connect practical `ggplot2` work with the principles of clear and responsible visualisation.

We will:

- start with the Week 2 files and a short `ggplot2` walkthrough
- complete an exploratory scatterplot exercise
- use Anscombe's quartet and the Datasaurus Dozen to show why plots matter
- discuss media examples where design choices shape interpretation
- finish with a checklist of visualisation principles and common pitfalls

<p class="take-home">By the end of the session, take away that plots help us reason about evidence. They can reveal patterns, question summaries, and communicate findings, but design choices also shape what people believe.</p>


## What is data visualisation?

- Using graphics to understand data
- Using graphics to communicate evidence
- Exploratory: what patterns are in the data?
- Explanatory: what should the audience take away?

Common plot types:

- scatterplots, line plots, bar plots
- histograms, boxplots, density plots
- pie charts, maps, heatmaps

## Discuss in pairs (2 mins)

What is the first thing you notice in each plot? What did you learn from it?

```{r pair-discussion-plots, echo=FALSE, fig.width=9, fig.height=4, out.width="90%"}
d_modality <- summarise(d_vocab,
                        rt = mean(rt),
                        .by = modality)

p_bar <- ggplot(data = d_modality,
                mapping = aes(x = modality, y = rt)) +
  geom_col(fill = "grey70", colour = "grey30", width = 0.65) +
  labs(x = "Response modality",
       y = "Average reaction time (ms)") 

p_scatter <- ggplot(data = d_vocab,
                    mapping = aes(x = ppt_vocab,
                                  y = rt,
                                  colour = modality)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.45) +
  stat_smooth(method = "lm", se = FALSE) +
  labs(x = "Vocabulary score",
       y = "Average reaction time (ms)",
       colour = "Response modality") +
  theme(legend.position = "top")

p_bar + p_scatter + plot_annotation(tag_levels = "A")
```


## Building up a plot: data and aesthetics

```
</div>

       aes(x = ppt_vocab, y = rt)) +
  theme(text = element_text(size = 15),

```

## A more polished version

We can add labels, colour choices, and a cleaner theme later.

```{r ggplot-build-polished, echo=FALSE, fig.width=6, fig.height=4, out.width="60%"}
ggplot(data = d_vocab,
       mapping = aes(x = ppt_vocab,
                     y = rt,
                     colour = modality,
                     linetype = modality)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.35) +
  stat_smooth(method = "lm", se = FALSE, fullrange = T) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::comma) +
  ggthemes::scale_color_colorblind() +
  labs(x = "Vocabulary score",
       y = "Average reaction time (ms)",
       colour = "Response modality",
       linetype = "Response modality") +
  ggthemes::theme_clean(base_size = 14) +
  theme(legend.position = "top",
        legend.justification = "right")
```

## What to recognise today

<div style="float: left; width: 32%; font-size: 82%; line-height: 1.15;">

- `data = ...`: which dataset should R use?
- `aes(...)`: which variables go on the plot?
- `geom_point()`: draw points
- `stat_smooth()`: add a trend line
- `labs()`: write clearer labels

</div>

## Creating an exploratory plot

**15 minutes:** work on **1_scatterplots.Rmd**

Aim: complete the main blanks, render the document, and write short interpretations.

Start in class and finish at home if needed.


## Why data visualisation? {.smaller}

> "[data visualisation] forces us to notice what we never expected to see." [@tukey1977exploratory]

Behavioural data are usually noisy and full of individual differences. A good visualisation helps us ask better questions before decide for a summary or model.

- **See what summaries hide:** distributions, clusters, outliers, and non-linear patterns
- **Check the story:** does the plot support the claim made by the mean, correlation, or model?
- **Choose better analyses:** visual patterns can suggest transformations, grouping variables, or model problems
- **Communicate responsibly:** design choices can make effects look larger, smaller, clearer, or more uncertain

<p class="take-home">Plots are not decoration. They are part of how we reason about evidence.</p>



## Anscombe's quartet [@anscombe1973graphs]


```{r echo = F, results="asis"}
anscombe <- pivot_longer(data = datasets::anscombe, 
             cols = everything(),
             names_to = c(".value", "Set"),
             names_pattern = "(.)(.)") 

ac_tab <- anscombe %>%
  nest(c(x,y)) %>%
  mutate(x_mean = map(data, ~mean(.$x)),
         x_sd = map(data, ~sd(.$x)),
         y_mean = map(data, ~mean(.$y)),
         y_sd = map(data, ~sd(.$y)),
         model = map(data, ~lm(y ~ x, data = .)),
         intercept = map(model, ~coef(.)[1]),
         slope = map(model, ~coef(.)[2]),
         cor = map(data, ~cor(.$y, .$x))) %>% 
  select(-data, -model) %>% 
  unnest(-Set) %>% 
  mutate(across(where(is.numeric), round, 2)) %>% 
  select(Set, starts_with("x"), starts_with("y"), Correlation = cor, Intercept = intercept, Slope = slope) 

ac_tab %>%
  kable("html", align = rep("c",3), 
        col.names = c("Data set", "Mean", "SD", "Mean", "SD", "Correlation", "Intercept", "Slope")) %>%
  kable_styling(bootstrap_options = c("striped", "hover", "responsive"), 
                font_size = 18, full_width = T) %>%
  add_header_above(c(" ", "x" = 2, "y" = 2, "y ~ x" = 3))
```


## Anscombe's quartet 

```{r echo = F, out.width="75%"}
anscombe %>% 
  rename(`Data set` = Set) %>% 
  ggplot(aes(y = y, x = x)) +
  facet_wrap(~`Data set`, labeller = label_both) +
  scale_y_continuous(limits = c(0, 17)) +
  scale_x_continuous(limits = c(0, 20)) +
  stat_smooth(method = "lm", se = T, fullrange = T, colour = "red") +
  theme_bw() +
  theme(strip.text = element_text(hjust = 0, face = "bold"))
```


## Anscombe's quartet 

```{r echo = F, out.width="75%"}
anscombe %>% rename(`Data set` = Set) %>% 
  ggplot(aes(y = y, x = x)) +
  facet_wrap(~`Data set`, labeller = label_both) +
  stat_smooth(method = "lm", se = T, fullrange = T, colour = "red", size = .5) +
  geom_point(color = "blue") +
  scale_y_continuous(limits = c(0, 17)) +
  scale_x_continuous(limits = c(0, 20)) +
  theme_bw() +
  theme(strip.text = element_text(hjust = 0, face = "bold"))
```


## How is this possible?

Summary statistics are constraints, not fingerprints.

- A mean only fixes the balance point of the values.
- A standard deviation only fixes the average spread around that balance point.
- A correlation or regression line only describes the average linear association.
- None of these summaries says where each point has to be.

Many different point patterns can satisfy the same constraints. Anscombe's quartet was constructed to demonstrate this. The Datasaurus Dozen was generated by moving points while keeping key summaries nearly unchanged [@matejka2017same].

<p class="take-home">Summaries can be correct and still incomplete. The plot shows the structure that the summaries leave out.</p>


## The datasaurus dozen | @matejka2017same: [see link](https://www.autodeskresearch.com/publications/samestats)

**15 minutes:** Open RMarkdown document **2_tdd.Rmd**

Aim: compare summary statistics with the plotted data.

Finish at home if needed.






## Visualisation is not neutral

Anscombe's quartet and the Datasaurus Dozen make the same point:

- the same summary statistics can describe very different data
- a mean, standard deviation, correlation, or model line can hide the pattern
- plotting the data can reveal outliers, clusters, curves, and unusual cases
- the visualisation changes what we notice and what we think needs explaining

<p class="take-home">Plots are not decoration after the analysis. They are part of how we understand the data.</p>

## How plots shape beliefs

Next, we will look at examples from media and public communication.

For each example, ask:

- what does the plot make easy to believe?
- what design choice creates that impression?
- what information is missing, hidden, or emphasised?
- how could the plot be changed to support a fairer comparison?

<p class="take-home">Design choices can persuade or mislead, even when the numbers are real [@pandey2014persuasive].</p>

## Pair activity: media examples

**5 minutes preparation**

Each pair takes one example. Be ready to tell us:

- what the plot makes easy to believe
- which design choice creates that impression
- how you would improve it

1. [Truncated y-axis in a cable-news chart](https://www.mediamatters.org/fox-news/updated-worst-chart-ive-seen-all-day)
2. [Pie chart for responses that add up to more than 100%](https://flowingdata.com/2009/11/26/fox-news-makes-the-best-pie-chart-ever/)
3. [Election maps and the problem that land does not vote](https://storymaps.arcgis.com/stories/0e636a652d44484b9457f953994b212b)
4. [Reuters Florida gun-deaths chart with an inverted axis](https://www.livescience.com/45083-misleading-gun-death-chart.html)

## Pair activity: main points

- **Truncated y-axis:** small numerical changes can look dramatic when the baseline is hidden.
- **Wrong chart type:** a pie chart implies parts of one whole, so it misleads when categories overlap or add to more than 100%.
- **Election maps:** large areas can look more important than densely populated areas.
- **Inverted axis:** reversing the axis can make increases look like decreases.

<p class="take-home">Visual design choices, data choices, and wording can change the story people see.</p>

## Same numbers, different beliefs {.columns-2}

A bar can make the mean look like a container for the data.

Viewers can treat values inside the bar as more likely than equally distant values outside it [@correll2014error].


Better alternative: show the distribution, not only the summary.

\columnbreak

```{r belief-example, echo=FALSE, fig.width=5.2, fig.height=4.6}
set.seed(40940)
d_belief <- tibble(
  condition = rep("Condition A", 160),
  score = rnorm(160, mean = 54, sd = 11)
)

mean_score <- mean(d_belief$score)
se_score <- sd(d_belief$score) / sqrt(nrow(d_belief))
summary_belief <- tibble(
  condition = "Condition A",
  mean_score = mean_score,
  lower = mean_score - 1.96 * se_score,
  upper = mean_score + 1.96 * se_score
)

p_bar <- ggplot(summary_belief, aes(x = condition, y = mean_score)) +
  geom_col(fill = "grey75", colour = "grey30", width = 0.55) +
  geom_errorbar(aes(ymin = lower, ymax = upper), width = 0.12) +
  coord_cartesian(ylim = c(0, 70)) +
  labs(title = "Summary only", x = NULL, y = "Score") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 13) +
  theme(axis.text.x = element_blank())

p_dist <- ggplot(d_belief, aes(x = condition, y = score)) +
  geom_jitter(width = 0.12, alpha = 0.35, size = 1.2, colour = "#2c7fb8") +
  geom_hline(yintercept = mean_score, linewidth = 1, colour = "#d95f0e") +
  coord_cartesian(ylim = c(0, 70)) +
  labs(title = "Distribution visible", x = NULL, y = "Score") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 13) +
  theme(axis.text.x = element_blank())

p_bar + p_dist + plot_annotation(tag_levels = "A")
```

## Encoding choices matter {.columns-2}

Cleveland and McGill showed that some visual comparisons are easier than others [@cleveland1984graphical].

Easier:

- position on a common scale
- aligned lengths

Harder:

- angles
- areas
- colour intensity

\columnbreak

```{r encoding-example, echo=FALSE, fig.width=5.2, fig.height=4.6}
d_encode <- tibble(
  category = c("A", "B", "C", "D"),
  value = c(34, 37, 49, 58)
)

p_dot <- ggplot(d_encode, aes(x = value, y = category)) +
  geom_point(size = 3, colour = "#2c7fb8") +
  scale_x_continuous(limits = c(0, 65)) +
  labs(title = "Position", x = "Value", y = NULL) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 13)

p_bubble <- ggplot(d_encode, aes(x = category, y = 1, size = value)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.65, colour = "#d95f0e") +
  scale_size_area(max_size = 18) +
  labs(title = "Area", x = NULL, y = NULL, size = "Value") +
  theme_void(base_size = 13) +
  theme(legend.position = "none",
        plot.title = element_text(hjust = 0.5))

p_dot + p_bubble + plot_annotation(tag_levels = "A")
```

## Principles for this module {.smaller}

<p class="take-home compact-take-home">A useful plot should help the viewer reason about the evidence, not just decorate the analysis.</p>

Drawing on exploratory data analysis and visualisation principles [@hartwig1979exploratory; @tufte1983visual; @cleveland1984graphical], use these checks:

- **Show the data and variation:** make distributions, outliers, clusters, and uncertainty visible where they matter.
- **Make comparisons easy:** arrange the plot around the question the viewer needs to answer.
- **Use scales honestly:** avoid truncated, inverted, unequal, or area-based encodings that distort effects.
- **Label enough for interpretation:** make variables, units, groups, and the intended comparison clear.
- **Remove competing design:** decoration, heavy gridlines, and excessive colour should not compete with the evidence.
- **Stay skeptical and open:** every plot is a choice; use visualisation for discovery, not only confirmation.

## Same data, different design

```{r design-comparison, echo=FALSE, fig.width=9, fig.height=4, out.width="90%"}
p_hidden <- summarise(d_vocab, rt = mean(rt), .by = modality) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = modality, y = rt)) +
  geom_col(fill = "grey75", colour = "grey30", width = 0.65) +
  coord_cartesian(ylim = c(1350, 1700)) +
  labs(title = "Summary + cropped axis",
       x = "Response modality",
       y = "Average reaction time (ms)") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 13)

p_visible <- ggplot(d_vocab, aes(x = modality, y = rt)) +
  geom_jitter(width = 0.12, alpha = 0.25, size = 1, colour = "#2c7fb8") +
  geom_boxplot(width = 0.35, outlier.shape = NA, alpha = 0.25) +
  labs(title = "Distribution visible",
       x = "Response modality",
       y = "Average reaction time (ms)") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 13)

p_hidden + p_visible + plot_annotation(tag_levels = "A")
```

What changes in your interpretation?

## Make comparisons easy

```{r comparison-easy, echo=FALSE, fig.width=9, fig.height=4, out.width="90%"}
d_vocab_2 <- summarise(d_spellname,
                       rt = mean(rt),
                       .by = c(ppt_id, ppt_vocab, cat, modality)) %>%
  drop_na()

p_hard <- d_vocab_2 %>%
  mutate(group = str_c(modality, cat, sep = "; ")) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = group, y = rt)) +
  geom_boxplot() +
  labs(title = "Harder comparison", x = NULL, y = "Average reaction time (ms)") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12) +
  theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1, vjust = 1))

p_easy <- ggplot(d_vocab_2, aes(x = modality, y = rt, colour = cat)) +
  geom_boxplot(outlier.alpha = 0.25) +
  labs(title = "Easier comparison", x = "Response modality", y = "Average reaction time (ms)",
       colour = "Category") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12) +
  theme(legend.position = "top")

p_hard + p_easy + plot_annotation(tag_levels = "A")
```

<p class="take-home">Good plots make the intended comparison visually easy.</p>

## Use labels to reduce effort

<div style="float: left; width: 45%;">

Good labels answer:

- What is measured?
- What are the units?
- What do colours or groups mean?
- What should the viewer compare?

</div>

<div style="float: right; width: 50%;">
```{r label-example, echo=FALSE, fig.width=4.8, fig.height=3.8, out.width="95%"}
ggplot(d_vocab, aes(x = ppt_vocab, y = rt, colour = modality)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.35) +
  stat_smooth(method = "lm", se = FALSE) +
  labs(x = "Vocabulary score",
       y = "Average reaction time (ms)",
       colour = "Response modality") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 13) +
  theme(legend.position = "top")
```
</div>

## Common visualisation pitfalls

Use the principles as a checklist when judging plots.


| Pitfall | Why it matters | Principle |
|---|---|---|
| Truncated or inverted axes | changes apparent size or direction of effects | avoid distortion |
| Overplotting | hides density and individual observations | show the data |
| Poor chart type | makes the wrong comparison easy | make comparisons easy |
| Too much decoration | competes with the evidence | remove competing design |
| Missing uncertainty | makes estimates look more precise | show the data and variation |
| Weak labels or legends | increases interpretation effort | label enough for interpretation |

## What's wrong with these? (1)

**If time: 2 minutes in pairs** which pitfall is most important in each example.

```{r bad-examples-1, fig.cap="", fig.width=8, fig.height=3, out.width="78%", echo=FALSE}
plot_example_image <- function(path) {
  image_read(path) %>%
    image_trim(fuzz = 8) %>%
    image_border("white", "8x8") %>%
    image_ggplot() +
    theme(plot.margin = margin(0, 0, 0, 0))
}

p_bad_a <- plot_example_image("gfx/bubbles.png")
p_bad_b <- plot_example_image("gfx/spss.png")

p_bad_a + p_bad_b +
  plot_annotation(tag_levels = "A") &
  theme(plot.margin = margin(0, 0, 0, 0))
```

::: {.figure-source}
Sources: A: @ke2024simultaneous; B: @rubiah2024effect.
:::
